meta.title: Incremental Online Learning on the European Space Agency Benchmark for Anomaly Detection in Satellite Telemetry

abstract: Ensuring safe and continuous spacecraft operation requires reliable satellite telemetry health monitoring, yet manual inspection of high dimensional telemetry streams is labor intensive and error prone. Automatic anomaly detection is therefore essential for autonomous spacecraft operations and a central component of the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Artificial Intelligence for Automation (A2I) initiative. The "European Space Agency Benchmark for Anomaly Detection in Satellite Telemetry" (ESA-ADB) provides a standardized research framework with real mission data, expert annotations, dedicated evaluation metrics, and baseline anomaly detection results. Although the benchmark establishes consistent evaluation, its baseline relies on static training without model updates during inference and therefore does not explicitly address concept drift in long running telemetry streams. This work investigates incremental online learning on ESA-ADB using modified versions of Mondrian Forest and Efficient Incremental Local Outlier Factor (EILOF), both designed for streaming updates and scalable to large numbers of telemetry channels. Our results demonstrate that online adaptation significantly improves performance in the most important metric (EW F0.5) compared to static training. We analyzed a sliding-window strategy for EILOF to balance adaptivity and stability. This analysis provides insights into memory constraints and computational trade-offs relevant for potential on-board deployment scenarios.

blocks.html: Reliable health monitoring is a prerequisite for the safe and uninterrupted operation of spacecraft. Modern satellites generate large volumes of high dimensional telemetry data over extended mission lifetimes, making manual inspection increasingly infeasible and error prone. As a result, automated anomaly detection has become a key component of autonomous satellite operations [1]. To support systematic research in this area, the European Space Agency Benchmark for Anomaly Detection in Satellite Telemetry (ESA-ADB) provides a comprehensive dataset based on real satellite missions together with carefully curated anomaly annotations and a standardized evaluation framework. While the benchmark offers valuable reference results for a selection of anomaly detection methods, its experimental protocol follows a strictly offline paradigm. Models are trained once on a designated training set and subsequently applied to streamed test data without any form of model adaptation. This setting does not fully reflect operational conditions, as satellite telemetry is subject to concept drift caused by aging hardware, changing operational modes, and evolving environmental influences [1]. This work investigates whether incorporating online learning into anomaly detection models can improve performance on the ESA benchmark. To this end, modified versions of Mondrian Forest [2] and the Efficient Incremental Local Outlier Factor (EILOF) [3] are evaluated in a fully online inference setting, where models are continuously updated as new telemetry samples arrive. In contrast to the benchmark setup, the training data is used only for hyperparameter selection and threshold calibration, thereby preserving an unsupervised learning scenario. Furthermore, a sliding window strategy is employed for EILOF to limit memory usage and to explore suitability for future on-board applications. The experimental results demonstrate that online model adaptation can substantially improve event wise anomaly detection performance on both benchmark missions. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for concept drift in satellite telemetry and provide evidence that incremental learning approaches represent a promising direction for operational anomaly detection systems.

With the ESA-ADB, prevalent flaws of publicly available anomaly detection datasets, like triviality and unrealistic anomaly density, are addressed. The dataset in ESA-ADB consists of telemetry data of two real satellite missions, referred to as Mission 1 and Mission 2. It comprises multiple pre-selected channels of different subsystems, which limits the large dimensionality of potentially thousands of channels in satellite telemetry. Table 1 provides an overview of the dataset. The channels are grouped to subsystems, but both, the channels and subsystems, are anonymized due to security reasons and thus fostering general data-driven approaches. An extensive, iterative manual annotation process, assisted by different anomaly detection methods, was conducted to create the ground truth. Finally, the subdatasets for both missions are divided into a training and test set of similar size. The provided evaluation metrics can be divided into subsystem/channel aware metrics and into subsystem/channel independent metrics. This work focuses on the latter since the anomaly score evaluations of the methods subject to this work do not automatically differentiate between subsystems or channels, just as many of the benchmark methods of ESA-ADB. The metrics conduct an event-wise evaluation, which results in every anomaly event having the same weight in the evaluation, independent of their length. Each metric focuses on an isolated evaluation of specific aspects. This results in four main metrics: 1. Corrected event-wise F0.5-score (EW F0.5, consisting of EW Precision and EW Recall), 2. Event-wise alarming precision (Alarming Precision), 3. Anomaly detection timing quality curve (ADTQC),

4. Modified affiliation-based F0.5-score (AFF F0.5, consisting of AFF Precision and AFF Recall). The different aspects these metrics assess are: 1. Minimizing false detections and maximizing correctly detected anomalies, 2. Reporting exactly one detection per anomaly, 3. Determining the anomaly start time as precisely as possible, 4. Finding the exact duration of the anomaly. This order also represents the prioritization established in ESA-ADB for an hierarchical evaluation. All metric scores are bounded by 0 and 1, where 1 depicts the optimal value [1].

blocks.html: The Mondrian Forest is an online tree ensemble method with the property of distributional equivalence between batch and incremental training. It partitions the feature space using data dependent splits and supports efficient updates without retraining [2]. The extension to the Isolation Mondrian Forest enables its use for anomaly detection, by combining the approach with the Isolation Forest. Each tree in the ensemble is grown until every leaf node contains only a single data point, which is required to determine an anomaly score. The anomaly score basically depends on the ratio of the average path length of the respective data point over the trees in the ensemble to the estimated general average path length in the ensemble [4]. Due to the principle of isolation, the most informative splits with respect to anomalies are expected to occur at relatively shallow depths in the trees rather than near the bottom of fully grown trees. Fully growing the trees therefore introduces additional memory and computational costs without yielding a significant gain in information. Consequently, in the experiments conducted in this work, a version of the Mondrian Forest is applied that retains the budget parameter λ, which controls the maximum tree depth and thus the associated memory and computational requirements, and an alternative anomaly score is employed. This score remains closely related to the average isolation depth while no longer requiring full isolation of every data point and has also proven to be more stable. As a result, the anomaly score is no longer bounded between 0 and 1. Furthermore, in our employed version of the Mondrian Forest, the axisaligned split operation for partitioning the feature space is replaced by hyperplane splits, as brought up in [2]. By that, we address possible artifacts regarding the anomaly scores resulting from axis-aligned splits, that in certain situations can cause data points getting assigned systematically too low anomaly scores, and clear anomalies may therefore no longer be detected. Hyperplane splits allow a split along multiple dimensions simultaneously, which provides more flexibility and thus these systematic artifacts should no longer occur [5]. The Efficient Incremental Local Outlier Factor (EILOF) is a density based method designed for streaming scenarios [3]. It builds on the original Local Outlier Factor (LOF), which is not equipped with an incremental component, so for adding new arriving observations from a data stream to the model, the whole model would have to be built from scratch, which is time consuming and not feasible in such a large scale data setting at hand [6]. An extension of the LOF, the incremental LOF, provides exactly such an incremental step, as well as a delete operation for removing observations from the model [7]. These two operations only update parameters and scores of observations in the model, that are actually affected by the incremental step or deletion, which limits the number of operations. In addition, in EILOF even more operations are omitted, since in a data stream we might only care about the current anomaly score of the new arriving observation and not about the newly updated anomaly scores of observations from the past. In fact, so many operations are omitted that the evaluation of the latest observation is not guaranteed to be consistent with the results of the original LOF applied to the current state of the data stream. In this work, a modified variant of EILOF is employed that more closely follows the original LOF formulation with respect to evaluating the most recently arriving observation in a data stream. The method is implemented in PyTorch [8], which enables GPU acceleration. As the model expands with each incoming observation, computational runtime and memory consumption remain critical challenges for maintaining real time capability. Therefore, a sliding window strategy is employed for EILOF. Before a new observation from the data stream is processed, the oldest observation within the current window is removed from the model. As a result, the model consistently retains exactly the number of observations defined by the predefined window size, except during the initial phase in which the window must first be filled. Constraining the model size in this manner also constitutes a step toward potential on board deployment. Finally, it should be noted that, as it is the case for our version of the Mondrian Forest, the anomaly scores of EILOF are not bounded by a general fix upper bound. So for both methods some sort of threshold tuning is required to provide a binary response. For the rest of this work we just refer to the modified versions of both methods as Mondrian Forest and EILOF.

blocks.html: Figure 1 illustrates the differences in the training and inference approaches between ESA-ADB and this work. In ESA- ADB, the benchmark methods are trained on the training data, considering the data labels to calculate contamination levels, means, and standard deviations, for example. Test data are streamed to compute anomaly scores without model updates and hence not accounting for potential concept drift [1]. However, in our approach, the training set serves solely for hyperparameter adjustment and anomaly score threshold selection. This preserves the un-supervised setting. For inference, the test data is streamed and in the beginning a small warm-up phase is used to build the models, without providing stable anomaly scores or any at all. Each training and test sub-dataset is scaled channel-wise based on the minimum and maximum values observed during the respective warm-up phase. After warm-up, anomaly scores are computed and models are updated online, enabling adaptation to concept drift. For Mondrian Forest, the number of trees and budget size were tuned. For EILOF, the number of k neighbors and sliding window size were selected. Thresholds were determined per sub-dataset via iterative evaluation of performance metrics.

The experiments were conducted on the following machine: Nvidia RTX A6000 GPU (49 GB VRAM), Intel Xeon W9- 3475X CPU 2.20 GHz, and 502 GB RAM. This sets the upper bounds for the models’ memory requirements, which were not fully utilized. This configuration exceeds the capabilities of a ‘standard PC’ used in the ESA-ADB experiments. However, the resources used here should still be realistic and feasible for AD in such a professional context as autonomous satellite health monitoring.

Regarding the model choice of EILOF on the train set, it was surprising that the smallest sliding window size of 25 000 observations, chosen from 25 000, 50 000, 100 000, always performed at least as well as the larger ones, and in some cases even slightly better. Table 2 and Table 3 present the results of the model evaluations on the test set in comparison with the best unsupervised and semi-supervised benchmark method of ESA-ADB regarding each of the four metrics. In addition to the four event-wise metrics, also the precision and recall values for both F0.5-based metrics are reported, providing additional insight for interpretation. Examining EW Precision and EW Recall reveals that the benchmark methods in most of the cases achieve high or comparatively high EW Recall scores but extremely low EW Precision scores, whereas Mondrian Forest and EILOF show a more balanced relationship between the two. This indicates that the benchmark methods flag a large number of anomalous events. Consequently, they identify many true positives and thereby reduce the number of false negatives, which leads to high recall. However, apparently this behavior also generates a substantial number of false positives, which in turn drastically lowers precision. Regarding Alarming Precision, in Mission 1 there is still a superiority from Mondrian Forest and EILOF against the benchmark methods visible, while for Mission 2 Teleman-ESA-Pruned clearly outperforms all other methods. With respect to ADTQC, again, for Mission 1 both custom AD methods outperform the benchmark methods, while for Mission 2 the metric scores are mostly very close to each other. Finally, examining the AFF F0.5 scores, it can be observed that, in both missions, none of the two custom methods has a significant advantage and both are partially outperformed, albeit narrowly. The runtimes of Mondrian Forest for computing the presented results ranged from 5 to 12.5 hours, while those of EILOF ranged from 4 to 10 hours. These runtimes are not analyzed in further detail, as exclusive access to the computational resources was not ensured during the experiments. However, when the actual temporal scale of several years and the sampling frequencies of the datasets are taken into account, the observed runtimes clearly demonstrate that both approaches are capable of real-time operation.

Overall, a consistent, significant superiority of Mondrian Forest and EILOF is only visible for EW F0.5, regarding the remaining three metrics the picture is mixed. Nevertheless, this can be regarded a strong result. With good cause EW F0.5 is assigned the highest priority in ESA-ADB, since it measures the actual anomaly event detection ability of the AD methods, which is the requirement for then looking at the timing quality, the number of redundant detections or the detection coverage in the next step. Considering the latter three aspects in isolation distorts the overall evaluation of the methods’ performance. Particularly noteworthy is, that Mondrian Forest and EILOF are able to cope with the relatively large number of channels. ESA-ADB contains also results for the benchmark methods trained and tested only on lightweight subsets of channels for both missions. Some methods do perform really well on these subsets with regard to EW F0.5. Teleman-ESA-Pruned, for example, reaches scores of 0.786 and 0.842. Thereby it must be noted, that their might be a bias introduced towards this method, since the iterative annotation process of the dataset heavily relies on the underlying Telemanom algorithm [9]. But still, it scales very poorly to the full set of channels, as seen in Table 2 and Table 3. Particularly interesting is that without reliance on train data and even with a very limited data history through the sliding window approach, it is possible to achieve such a performance improvement regarding the event-wise anomaly detection. In combination with the mostly very low EW Precision values of the benchmark methods, this strongly indicates that the present concept drift requires model adaption through online learning and less reliance solely on the train data. Moreover, the success of the sliding window approach depicts a step towards potential on-board applications. While it still might be necessary to keep a larger data history for detecting certain anomalies, it could play its part in an ensemble approach of on-board and on-ground anomaly detection.
